Identify the most likely WORKING etiological diagnosis or mechanism, and distinguish it from confirmed findings. An unavailable confirmatory test is neither a negative nor a positive result. Do not discard a well-supported leading cause solely because a confirmatory test is unavailable; equally, do not invent a cause if the information does not support ranking one. In reasoning, clearly label uncertainty, unexplained features, and what test or follow-up would confirm or change the leading hypothesis. Do not claim a requested protocol, timing, specimen or dynamic test was performed unless the returned source establishes it. Rank by the features together, including temporal pattern, medication and exposure history, and what is normal. State one most likely working diagnosis in diagnosis; retain syndrome and verified findings in reasoning. Put ONE JSON object serialized as a string in content: {"diagnosis":str,"reasoning":str,"confidence":number0-1,"unconfirmed":[str],"next_steps":[str]}. Diagnosis under60words; reasoning under180words. No new findings, internet, tools or reference answers.

review.diagnosis: Probable MRSA coronary stent infection causing an infected coronary pseudoaneurysm, with suspected associated purulent pericarditis and confirmed cardiac tamponade.
review.reasoning: Documented MRSA bacteremia, angiographic disruption of a prior coronary stent with a rapidly enlarging pseudoaneurysm, and turbid yellow pericardial fluid together strongly favor infection involving the stented coronary segment. Confirmed findings include new left-ventricular wall-motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion progressing to tamponade, and rapidly deteriorating circulation. Tamponade explains a major component of shock; associated coronary compromise may explain ventricular dysfunction, but infarction is unconfirmed. Pericardial infection is strongly suspected, whereas pseudoaneurysm rupture or communication with the pericardium is not established. Unavailable pericardial cultures, operative findings, and tissue cultures neither confirm nor exclude infection. Endocarditis remains unevaluated because TEE was unavailable. Stent timing, antibiotic identity, and exposure history are unknown; no pertinent normal results were provided. Operative inspection and coronary/stent and pericardial microbiology would confirm or revise the proposed mechanism.
unconfirmed: MRSA infection of coronary stent or arterial tissue
Myocardial infarction; ECG and troponin unavailable

Verify current antibiotics and allergy records; ensure intravenous MRSA-active treatment guided by available susceptibilities.
Obtain operative findings and coronary tissue, stent material, and pericardial cultures when feasible without delaying treatment.
Repeat blood cultures to establish clearance and echocardiography to reassess effusion and ventricular function; obtain TEE when feasible to assess endocarditis.
